html:
The Late Bronze Age collapse was the fall of most of the great states of the eastern Mediterranean within about fifty years, around 1200 to 1150 BCE. A world of palaces, kings who wrote letters to each other, and long-distance trade in copper and tin broke apart.

  • The Hittite kingdom in Anatolia vanished, and its capital Hattusa was abandoned.
  • The palaces of Mycenaean Greece were burned, and writing disappeared from Greece for centuries.
  • Ugarit and other trading cities on the Syrian coast were destroyed.
  • Egypt survived. Ramesses III fought off invaders known as the Sea Peoples, but Egypt came out weaker and lost its empire in the Levant.
  • Assyria also survived, shrunken.

The causes are still argued over. Candidates include drought and famine, earthquakes, raids and migrations by the Sea Peoples, revolts, and the breakdown of trade. Most historians now think several of these hit at once, and that tightly linked palace economies could not absorb so many shocks together.

What came after was a poorer, simpler age, often called the dark age in Greece. But it opened room for new players. Iron spread as a working metal, the Phoenician cities took over sea trade and spread the alphabet, and small kingdoms like Israel and Judah rose in the hills.
